title: Dead Band — Chapter 3: The Rules We Kept
weather: Cold rain easing; wet ground and gusts along the ridge
intro: Mara is back on the air. Her voice is tired but steady. The old county relay station may restore reliable coverage across the valley. It still has its battery bank, AC power supply, feed line, and tower—but it has been abandoned for months. Before anyone powers it up or touches the tower, the crew is going to inspect it. Today is a briefing, not a repair job. Get your notebook. You need to understand two things before you operate: how not to hurt yourself, and how to share the air with everyone else.

assignment.text: K7DBN, K7MVR. Good to hear you again. Yesterday you found me across the ridge. Now we need to bring the old county relay station back into service. It could give the valley a reliable link again. But the battery bank, mains supply, coax, and tower have all been sitting out here. We are not switching anything on or climbing anything until it has been inspected.

responses.text: K7MVR, K7DBN. Why is there a separate briefing before the work begins?

why-rules.text: “Two reasons. First, electricity and antennas can injure you even when the equipment looks harmless. Second, radios are a shared resource. The old FCC is gone, but we kept its Amateur Radio Service rules—Part 97—as our network charter. Not because someone is waiting to issue fines, but because the rules let strangers share the same air without turning every channel into a shouting match. Elias will brief you on power safety. Contact him on 147.500 MHz FM; listen first, then call him when the frequency is clear.”

battery-bank.text: K7DBN, K7ELN. Start with the battery bank. A 12-volt storage battery can deliver enormous current. If a metal tool bridges its terminals, it can become red-hot and cause severe burns, fire, or even an explosion. That is different from an ordinary electric shock: current passing through your body can heat tissue, disrupt the electrical functions of cells, and cause involuntary muscle contractions. Never let your body become the path between points at different voltages. Don’t improvise a short-circuit test.

responses.text: Copy, K7ELN. What should I look for in the station’s wiring and fuses?

fuses-and-wiring.text: “A fuse is a safety link. It opens the circuit when excessive current flows. Use the specified rating—never replace a 5-amp fuse with a 20-amp fuse or bypass it. The larger fuse may let the wiring overheat and start a fire. Use wires, connectors, and other components rated for the voltage and current they must carry; parts are not interchangeable just because they fit. In a 120-volt AC cable, black is the hot conductor. A fuse or circuit breaker belongs in series with the hot conductor.”

responses.text: K7ELN, K7DBN. Does switching the power supply off make it safe to open?

stored-charge.text: “No. A power supply can contain filter capacitors that retain a dangerous charge after the switch is off. Don't open the supply or assume it is safe because it is unplugged. A trained person must verify that it is discharged. Use three-wire cords and plugs, and a common safety ground for AC-powered station equipment. Anyone measuring high voltage must use a meter and leads rated for that voltage.”

responses.text: Copy. What must be checked before reconnecting the antenna feed line?

grounding-and-lightning.text: “Grounding and lightning protection are part of the installation, not optional extras. External ground rods and earth connections must be bonded together. The coax lightning arrester belongs on a grounded panel near where the feed lines enter the building. Ground conductors should be short and direct, without sharp bends. Local electrical codes establish the grounding requirements. Don't invent a shortcut and call it a ground.”

tower-inspection.text: K7DBN, K7RTH. I’m watching the tower from a safe distance. We inspect this from the ground. Tower climbing is never a one-person job. It requires proper training, an approved climbing harness, appropriate tie-off at all times, and a helper or observer. Never climb alone. Look for overhead electrical wires. If the tower or antenna could fall and any part could come within 10 feet of power wires, the site is not safe. Never attach an antenna to a utility pole.

responses.text: K7RTH, K7DBN. What should we inspect on the tower’s mechanical supports and guy wires?

supports-and-grounding.text: “A crank-up tower must be retracted, or secured with its mechanical safety locks, before anyone climbs it. Safety wire through a guy-line turnbuckle prevents vibration from loosening it. Tower grounding must follow local electrical codes; the grounding system needs proper rods bonded to the tower and to one another. Lightning conductors should be short and direct, with no sharp bends. A tower is a structural system, not just a pole with an antenna on top.”

responses.text: K7RTH, K7DBN. Copy. Mark the tower no-climb and wait for a trained crew.

stop-work.text: “Good,” K7RTH replies. “Sometimes the safest repair is to stop. She will explain a hazard you cannot see or smell: RF exposure.”

radiation-type.text: K7DBN, K7NNA. Radio signals are non-ionizing radiation. They do not have enough energy to cause chemical changes in cells or damage DNA in the way ionizing radiation can. But non-ionizing does not mean harmless at every power level. Strong RF can heat body tissue. Touching an antenna while it is transmitting can cause an RF burn.

responses.text: Ask what determines how much RF exposure a person receives.

exposure-factors.text: “Exposure depends on frequency, power, distance from the antenna, and the antenna's radiation pattern. Duty cycle is the percentage of time the transmitter is actually transmitting. A lower duty cycle reduces average exposure. Under the exposure-averaging rules, changing from a 100-percent to a 50-percent duty cycle doubles the allowable average power density. That is something to calculate, not an excuse to stand next to an antenna.”

responses.text: K7NNA, K7DBN. How does a station check and maintain RF safety compliance?

compliance.text: “Exposure limits vary with frequency because the human body absorbs RF energy differently at different frequencies. Compliance can be evaluated by calculation, computer modeling, or measurement with calibrated equipment. If the transmitter or antenna system changes, evaluate exposure again. Moving an antenna farther from people can reduce exposure. The station licensee is responsible for ensuring that no one is exposed above the FCC limits. Until this site has been evaluated, keep people away from the antenna whenever it transmits.”

stations.name: Valley Net Control (K7NCS) — The Network Charter

purpose-and-authority.text: K7DBN, this is K7NCS. Good to hear you again. Now the rules. Before the collapse, the FCC regulated the Amateur Radio Service; the ARRL was not the regulator. The service existed for self-training, advancing technical and communication skills, intercommunication, technical investigation, and public service. We kept the old FCC Part 97 rules as our charter. The spectrum belongs to no single operator. We share it, so we need common expectations.

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. How do the rules determine where and how each station may transmit?

spectrum-and-band-plans.text:
“Your license class determined which frequencies and modes you could use. Privileges varied by band segment and emission type; being authorized on a band did not mean every mode was allowed everywhere. Technician phone privileges on HF were limited to the 10-meter segment from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz. Some allocations were secondary, which meant amateurs had to avoid interfering with primary users. Do not transmit exactly at a band or sub-band edge: display error, transmitter drift, and modulation sidebands can put energy outside the authorized segment.

“A band plan was a voluntary guide for dividing a band among modes and activities. Local volunteer frequency coordinators, selected by area amateurs, recommended channels for repeaters and auxiliary stations; they did not replace the FCC or create legal frequency privileges. Propagation beacons were another special use: on 10 meters, automatically controlled amateur propagation beacons operated from 28.200 to 28.300 MHz. Technicians could also contact the International Space Station on VHF. The old rules set power ceilings—generally 200 watts PEP in Technician HF segments and 1,500 watts PEP above 30 MHz, subject to specific restrictions. Those were ceilings, not targets. Willful or malicious interference was prohibited; if two stations interfered, they were expected to coordinate and move rather than overpower one another.”

responses.text: Copy, K7NCS. What does the license itself grant, and when does it become valid?

licenses-and-callsigns.text: “Before the collapse, the FCC issued Technician, General, and Amateur Extra licenses. A license grant became effective when it appeared in the FCC Universal Licensing System database; a test-completion certificate by itself was not permission to transmit. The normal license term was ten years. Renewal could be requested up to 90 days before expiration. There was a two-year grace period after expiration, but an operator could not transmit until the license was renewed. Licensees had to keep their mailing address and email current so the FCC could reach them. Call signs were normally assigned sequentially, although any licensed amateur could request an available vanity call sign. International communication had to be incidental to Amateur Radio Service purposes or personal in character; operators could not contact a country whose administration had formally objected to such communications.”

responses.text: Copy. Who is responsible for controlling a station?

control-operator.text: “Every amateur station must have a control operator. The station licensee designates that operator, and the operator's license class determines the privileges used for the transmission. If the control operator is not the licensee, both share responsibility for proper operation. The control point is where the control-operator function is performed. Automatic control means the station can operate automatically under the rules—repeaters are an example. Remote control means an operator controls a station from another location, such as over the internet. Automatic does not mean uncontrolled.”

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. How do stations identify themselves and handle messages for others?

identification-and-third-party.text:
“Identify with your assigned callsign at least every ten minutes during a communication and at its end. Phone identification was in English, using a phone or CW emission. The phonetic alphabet was encouraged when speaking, especially when conditions were noisy. Tactical names such as ‘Valley Net’ were useful, but they did not replace the assigned callsign. Identify even when making test transmissions.

“A third-party communication was a message passed from one control operator to another on behalf of someone else. That was normal in message handling, but international third-party traffic required an agreement with the other country. If a repeater retransmitted an improper transmission, responsibility remained with the originating station’s control operator. A station and its records had to be made available for FCC inspection upon request. A club station license required at least four members.”

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. Test me: does the net name replace my callsign?

prohibited-transmissions.text: “Amateur frequencies were not for broadcasting to the general public, routine business, or messages encoded to obscure their meaning. Ordinary digital modes and procedural abbreviations were fine; encryption or secret codes intended to hide message content were generally prohibited, with a narrow exception for control commands to space stations or model craft. Obscene or indecent language was prohibited. Music was generally prohibited except when incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned-spacecraft communications. Operators generally could not be compensated for operating, with narrow exceptions such as communications that were part of classroom instruction at an educational institution. An occasional personal sale or trade of amateur equipment could be announced, but a regular sales business could not be run over the air.”

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. What is the rule about concealing a message’s meaning?

emergency-services.text: “An emergency did not erase every rule. Part 97 still applied; narrow exceptions allowed operation outside normal privileges when necessary for the immediate safety of human life or protection of property. ARES, the Amateur Radio Emergency Service, was a civilian volunteer service of licensed amateurs organized for public-service communications. RACES, the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service, was a separate civil-defense service under Part 97. A RACES control operator needed an amateur license and current enrollment certified by a civil-defense organization. ARES membership alone did not qualify someone to operate a RACES station.”

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. What does the emergency exception actually allow?

acknowledgement.text: “Report received, K7DBN,” K7NCS replies. “Good work. You listened to the net, waited for an opening, identified yourself, and passed a concise report. The old rules are not a ritual. They are how we keep a shared channel usable and how we know who is responsible for a station. We will not activate the county site until the qualified crew completes its inspection. You now know the safety limits and the operating charter. Tomorrow, we put that knowledge to work at the station.”

identification-correction.text: K7NCS: “No. Other operators and anyone monitoring the frequency must be able to identify the station transmitting. Use your assigned callsign at least every ten minutes and at the end.”

prohibited-check.text: K7NCS asks: “The Watchers may be listening. Can you hide the meaning of an ordinary amateur message with encryption or a secret code?”

responses.text: No. Use an allowed mode and plain, understandable message content; do not encode it to conceal the meaning.
responses.feedback: Correct. Ordinary digital modes are permitted, but messages generally may not be encoded to obscure their meaning.

responses.text: Yes. Encrypt the message so unauthorized listeners cannot understand it.
responses.feedback: The desire for privacy does not create a general encryption exception in amateur radio.

prohibited-correction.text: K7NCS: “That is exactly the temptation the rule is meant to prevent. Amateur transmissions are generally open. Do not use encryption or secret codes to hide message content.”

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. Understood; keep the message clear and use an authorized mode.
responses.feedback: You retained the rule: no concealed message content.

emergency-check.text: K7NCS asks: “Suppose lives are at risk. Does that mean every operating rule disappears?”

responses.text: No. The exception is narrow: depart from normal privileges only when immediately necessary to protect human life or property.
responses.feedback: Correct. An emergency can justify only the limited action needed for immediate safety.

responses.text: Yes. In an emergency, any frequency, power, or transmission is automatically allowed.
responses.feedback: An emergency is not a blanket suspension of every rule.

emergency-correction.text: K7NCS: “No. The exception is narrow and tied to immediate necessity. ARES and RACES provide organized public-service structures; they are not permission to ignore every rule.”

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. Understood; the emergency exception is limited.
responses.feedback: You corrected the misconception: an emergency does not cancel every operating rule.

final-report.text: K7NCS: “Good. Now pass the site status briefly and clearly so the net knows what is safe and what is not.”
